* US September PCE inflation rises to [3.6%](https://cryptobriefing.com/us-core-pce-inflation-rises-exceeding-forecast/) year over year, core hits 3.1%

* Franklin Templeton launches ETFs that reinvest stock dividends into a [5%](https://www.chooserich.live/story/franklin-templeton-stock-bitcoin-etfs-wex9z95) bitcoin allocation

* NVIDIA weighs billions in credit guarantees for Nscale's [460MW](https://www.chooserich.live/story/nvidia-weighs-nscale-credit-guarantees-fz8kc5t) Anthropic data center

* Ondo launches seven Intelligent Portfolios on Solana, three powered by [BlackRock](https://www.chooserich.live/story/ondo-solana-blackrock-portfolios-2xz7b8w)

* Polymarket switches to [cancel-only](https://www.chooserich.live/story/polymarket-frontend-exploit-drained-funds-gxju34s) mode amid unconfirmed wallet-drain reports

* Alphabet plunges [11.5%](https://x.com/Hedgeye/status/2115785692689166816) after Q3 earnings on slowing search growth

* US spot bitcoin ETFs post [$137.3M](https://www.chooserich.live/story/us-spot-bitcoin-etf-inflows-e5fx5b3) inflows, a third straight day of gains

* Amazon stock plunges after a Q3 earnings miss, erasing about [$315B](https://x.com/solidintel_x/status/2115897207672963260) in value

Hey, it's Adrian! “Fading macro uncertainty” has been a good mantra since the Bitcoin low in June. That’s why I kept building my portfolio with a more risk on stance since then, while accepting that the risks and the uncertainty were unlikely to clear anytime soon. The strategy has worked quite well. Ethena is up 59%, Zcash 62% and NEAR 164% since I started accumulating. But oil prices and bond yields remain elevated, and the stock market is feeling it. 59% of S&P 500 stocks are in a bear market, and 41% trade more than 30% below their highs. AI financing concerns are growing, and sentiment has shifted clearly bearish. Then the Fed held rates on Wednesday, with two members voting for a hike. Lovely. Which raises a few questions: Is more pain coming after the midterms next Tuesday? Will crypto go down if we see a proper correction in stocks? And if so, does my “early bull market” call need to be revisited? In the Alpha section I explain why I’m buying Galaxy, and before that, why the owner of the New York Stock Exchange just made my HYPE position a lot more interesting. ️ ⚡ On today's Episode: 📈 Macro Update – The Fed held at 3.75% to 4% with two votes for a hike, and the 10-year yield sits at 5.04%. Polymarket gives the Democrats 93% for the House and 68% for the Senate, and the S&P 500 was higher one year after each of the last ten midterms. 🔊 Crypto Pulse – Bitcoin sits at $81.5k, right on the ETF cost basis, after $423.6 million of ETF inflows in three sessions. The 50-week MA at $76.3k is the support I watch, 12% below the October high. trade[XYZ] and ICE, the owner of the NYSE, plan to bring Hyperliquid’s 24/7 perps to the US, with Stan Druckenmiller joining as an investor. HYPE jumped about 17% to $93.6. 🐂 Alpha Insights – I’m buying Galaxy (GLXY), a company worth about $6.8 billion that holds about $6.6 billion in cash, Treasuries, stablecoins and investments. The current state of the market. Market Overview Start with the Fed, because rates are what everything else hangs off right now. On Wednesday the Fed held rates at 3.75% to 4%. Two members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, voted for another quarter point hike after September’s. The statement says inflation “remains elevated”, and markets now price an 86% chance of a hike in December. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.04% after the decision. → That’s the pressure stocks are feelin

October brought some impressive numbers from India's IT industry. On October 8, TCS reported $3.1 billion in annualised AI revenue. Two weeks later, Infosys revealed that its AI business had grown 29% in a single quarter. Sounds like the start of another IT boom, right? Not quite. TCS reported just 2.4% year-on-year dollar revenue growth. Infosys grew 1.5% in constant currency and cut its full-year growth forecast to 1–2%. Billions coming in from AI, yet overall growth is barely moving. For decades, India's IT companies made money by putting skilled engineers on projects and charging clients for their time. Now the same technology they're selling is helping clients get work done in fewer hours. And that's where things get complicated. The Numbers Don't Quite Add Up October's earnings reports tell the story better than any industry prediction. So, why isn't all that AI money showing up in overall growth? Part of the answer lies in cautious client spending and tougher pricing. Businesses are still investing in technology, but they're questioning every major expense. And when a project becomes cheaper to deliver, clients naturally want a share of the savings. The Problem With Selling Hours Imagine a software company that charged a client for ten developers working over three months. A year later, the same team has coding assistants, automated testing, and tools that handle much of the routine documentation. The project finishes earlier, the client is happy, and the developers are more productive. But when the next contract arrives, the client asks for a lower price. Fair question. Difficult answer. Indian IT companies spent years growing by adding engineers to projects. Under hourly contracts, fewer working hours can mean less revenue. Fixed-price projects work differently, though. Finishing early can actually improve profits. Same technology. Two very different outcomes. A faster project doesn't always mean a bigger invoice. Sometimes, it means exactly the opposite. That's the uncomfortable reality the industry now has to deal with. Clients Aren't Looking for Another Chatbot Walk into a bank, hospital, or retail business, and you'll probably find work that still takes far too long. Bank employees checking customer documents, hospital staff answering the same questions, or retail teams struggling with inventory records.
